name: Scar tattooing / micropigmentation

card.summary: Cosmetic tattooing that deposits pigment in scars or pale skin to blend them with surrounding skin; documented clinically but with little outcome data.
card.aka: Medical tattooing, scar camouflage tattoo, dermal micropigmentation
card.note: Pigment is semi-permanent and matching skin tone is difficult; the Wikipedia overview gives no outcome data.

quick.overview:
Scar tattooing, or micropigmentation, places pigment into the skin to make scars, pale patches or missing structures such as an areola look more like the surrounding skin. It belongs to the broader field of medical tattooing.[1]
There is no controlled outcome data; the evidence base cited by Wikipedia consists mainly of patient satisfaction reviews and general reviews of medical tattooing.
quick.mechanism: A tattoo device deposits pigment in the dermis, in a realistic style meant to imitate normal skin color. For scars, people may alternatively choose a decorative design that covers the area.[1]
quick.risks: Wikipedia's article does not detail risks specific to scar camouflage. It notes that diabetes can impair wound healing, so timing and location of a medical tattoo may need care in people with diabetes.[1] General tattoo risks include infection and allergic reactions.

lead: Scar tattooing, also called micropigmentation, deposits skin-toned pigment into a scar or pale patch so the area blends with the surrounding skin. It is a form of medical (or paramedical) tattooing, which aims to hide a condition or the result of its treatment, usually in a realistic style.[1] People use it to make surgical scars, vitiligo patches, hair-transplant marks and missing areolas less noticeable, and the effect is an evener-looking skin surface without further surgery.[1][3][6]

A dermatology review describes micropigmentation as a semi-permanent camouflage technique used for stable vitiligo, for alopecia (including androgenetic alopecia and stable alopecia areata) and for semi-permanent makeup, and notes that knowledge of the indication and of colour theory matters for a natural-looking result.[3] The same family of methods includes scalp micropigmentation, where pigment dots imitate closely cut hair, and microblading, used to restore eyebrows lost to alopecia or trichotillomania.[1][5][6]

The best-known body of research is a 2021 PRISMA systematic review of medical tattooing, which found 18 studies covering baldness, vitiligo, scars from incisions, lacerations or burns and nipple-areola reconstruction, and reported high levels of patient satisfaction while calling for randomised trials and independent outcome assessment.[7] Within looksmaxxing discussion the method appears among non-surgical options for concealing scars and hair-transplant marks, with scalp micropigmentation compared against hair systems in forum threads.[12]

chain: Pigment is deposited in the dermis to match surrounding skin or hair
Contrast between scar or pale patch and normal skin is reduced
Scar, patch or bald area is less noticeable at conversational distance
angle.text: A practitioner tattoos pigment matched to the person's skin or hair colour into the scar or patch so it blends in. The change is cosmetic and is visible as soon as the area heals, though the pigment can fade and may need touch-ups.

paras: Medical tattoos are tattoos used to treat a condition, convey medical information or mark a body spot; paramedical tattoos conceal a condition or its treatment, for instance by recreating a nipple or areola after breast surgery.[1] Scar tattooing belongs to the second group and is usually done in a realistic style. For scars, people may alternatively choose a decorative cover-up design.[1] The technique is described in dermatology literature as novel and relatively easy to learn, relying on colour theory to choose pigments that approximate the surrounding skin.[3]

sections.h: How it is used to improve appearance
paras: For a scar, the usual goals are to reduce the colour difference between the scar and the skin around it, or, in hair-bearing areas, to imitate missing hair. Pale, depigmented scars and patches are the main targets because added pigment narrows the contrast; Wikipedia lists covering scars and simulating fingernails among documented uses.[1] A clinical trial registered as NCT04046679 examines a different approach to repigmenting achromic scars, a bleomycin infusion technique, which indicates that the problem of pale scars is under active study.[2]

Alternatives that people compare include surgical revision, laser treatment, hair transplantation (a 2022 case report describes about 2,600 scalp-harvested grafts used to treat a cheek burn scar in hair-bearing facial skin) and makeup or camouflage products.[16] Micropigmentation is positioned as a non-surgical option with little downtime.

Documented uses include covering scars and simulating fingernails, reducing the visibility of vitiligo patches, and replacing a removed areola or filling pigment loss after free nipple grafts following mastectomy, reconstruction, breast reduction or chest masculinisation.[1] Related microblading restores eyebrows lost to alopecia or trichotillomania.[1] Royal Derby Hospital began offering free nipple tattoos in 2011, according to Wikipedia.[1]

A 2023 review lists stable vitiligo, androgenetic alopecia, stable alopecia areata and semi-permanent makeup as the main dermatological indications.[3] A 2022 narrative review of vitiligo at the angle of the lips lists micropigmentation alongside grafting methods for an area that resists medical treatment.[10] A 2026 narrative review of nipple-areola reconstruction reports that tattooing offers high patient satisfaction with little downtime, with pigment fading described as common.[9]

Scalp micropigmentation, a close relative, places pigment in the upper skin layers in a stippling pattern that resembles closely cut hair, and is used to conceal hair loss.[5] Wikipedia's overview adds that it can also conceal hair-transplant scars and the marks of burns on the scalp, that a course usually takes three to four sessions of about two hours each, and that practitioners may patch-test for ink allergy.[6] It describes the hairline as one of the most crucial aspects of the treatment, notes that an improperly done hairline can look unnatural, and states that the pigment can be removed with laser.[6]

A 2025 series of ten patients with androgenetic or scarring alopecia who received a standardised three-session protocol reported high cosmetic density scores after treatment that declined modestly by six months, with more fading in scarring alopecia, high satisfaction and no adverse events; the authors called for larger long-term studies.[8] A 2022 case report correlated scalp micropigmentation findings on trichoscopy and histopathology.[5]

In a looksmax.org thread comparing scalp micropigmentation with hair systems, one member says micropigmentation suits people who always wear a shaved look, who have missing hairs after hair transplantation or who have diffuse thinning, and says hair systems are the better option for typical male pattern baldness; another replies that the skull must suit a buzzed look.[12]

Medical tattooing is old: Wikipedia notes that Ötzi, who lived around 3350 to 3105 BC, had joint tattoos that may have been therapeutic, and that Galen attempted corneal tattooing around 150 CE.[1] In 1835 the German doctor Pauli tattooed skin lesions including nevi with mercury sulfide and white lead, Louis de Wecker revived corneal tattooing in the 1870s, and lip scars were tattooed with cinnabar starting in 1911.[1] A 1996 article in Annals of Plastic Surgery titled Micropigmentation reflects the technique's place in plastic-surgery literature by the late twentieth century.[4] More recent coverage has focused on mastectomy tattoos, scalp micropigmentation and dermatological camouflage.[3][5][11]

A 2026 qualitative study interviewed 12 women who chose mastectomy tattoos, mostly after reconstruction, and reported themes of changed bodily perceptions, tattoos as a coping mechanism and tattoos as a reclaimed identity; the authors support including artistic tattooing in post-mastectomy care.[11] A review of dermatologic sequelae of cancer therapies lists scarring, persistent alopecia and pigmentary changes as lasting effects that are linked to anxiety and reduced quality of life, and describes procedural options for restoring appearance.[15]

Wikipedia's medical tattoo overview notes that diabetes can impair wound healing, so location and timing of a medical tattoo may need care in people with diabetes.[1] General tattoo considerations such as infection and allergy to ink apply, and practitioners of scalp micropigmentation may patch-test for ink allergy.[6] Pigment is semi-permanent, and matching it to skin tone is described as depending on the practitioner's colour skills.[3]

Case reports describe reactions to tattoo pigment in general, particularly red inks: one 2026 report describes a man whose red pigment was followed by multisystem granulomatosis over more than ten years, and a 2026 review discusses links between tattoo pigments and sarcoid-type granulomas while noting that causality remains unproven.[13][14] These reports concern decorative tattoos and are not specific to scar camouflage. Scalp pigment can be removed with laser treatment.[6]

No randomised controlled trials of scar tattooing as such were found. The 2021 systematic review of medical tattooing included 18 studies (at minimum case series) and reported high patient satisfaction, with a practice recommendation grade of B based on level III to IV evidence; its authors recommended clearer procedural reporting, standardised outcome measures, independent satisfaction ratings and randomised trials with waitlist controls.[7] Other literature consists of narrative reviews and case reports: a 2023 review of micropigmentation indications,[3] a 2022 case report on scalp micropigmentation,[5] a 2025 ten-patient series,[8] and a 1996 plastic surgery article.[4] A registered trial (NCT04046679) examines a bleomycin infusion technique to repigment achromic scars; it is a different method from tattooing.[2]

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing forums, micropigmentation comes up mostly as scalp micropigmentation for hair loss and hair-transplant marks, compared with hair systems and transplants.[12]

claims.claim: Scalp micropigmentation suits shaved looks, transplant marks and diffuse thinning
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says it helps only if you always wear a bald look, have gaps after FUE or have diffuse thinning, and that hair systems are better for typical male pattern baldness.[12]
claims.experts: A 2025 ten-patient series reported high cosmetic scores and satisfaction with some fading by six months, and Wikipedia lists hair-transplant and burn scars among its uses.[8][6]

claims.claim: Tattooing can blend a scar into surrounding skin
claims.believers: Practitioners and patients describe realistic pigment matching that makes scars, vitiligo patches and areolas less noticeable.[1][3]
claims.experts: A 2021 systematic review of 18 studies found high patient satisfaction but graded the evidence level III to IV and called for randomised trials.[7]

claims.believers: Scalp micropigmentation is described as permanent pigment that can be adjusted by touch-up.[6]
claims.experts: A 2023 review calls it semi-permanent, a 2025 series saw modest fading by six months and more in scarring alopecia, and a 2026 review calls fading common in areola tattoos.[3][8][9]

claims.claim: Colour matching is hard to get right
claims.believers: Reviews and practitioners say natural results depend on colour theory and the practitioner's skill.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes an improperly placed hairline can look unnatural, and the pigment can be removed by laser if needed.[6]

claims.believers: Case reports link red inks to granulomatous reactions in some people.[13]
claims.experts: A 2026 review notes causality between tattoo pigments and sarcoid granulomas is unproven; Wikipedia notes diabetes can impair wound healing.[14][1]
